node.label: J. L. Granatstein
node.date_label: Canada’s War (1975) · Broken Promises: with J. M. Hitsman (1977) · The Ottawa Men (1982) · Who Killed Canadian History? (1998)
node.description: A Canadian historian whose research connects wartime government, defence policy and military command. In a 2019 written interview he identifies the domestic politics of war and high command as his central interests, distinguishing them from battlefield narrative alone. His argument about the loss of national history also generated a historiographical dispute: the account here attributes that argument to A. B. McKillop’s critical reading and preserves the limits of the unread 1998 book.

proposed_edges.relationship: Connects military history to the domestic politics of wartime government and the politics of high command.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s written answer to “Why did you choose to focus so much of your work on Canada’s role in the world wars?” (2019). This is his research emphasis, not an endorsement of every military or political judgment in the interview.

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes the disputed charge that specialization and ideological commitments have displaced national history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: As characterized and challenged in A. B. McKillop’s 1999 abstract, already read in the graph. The polemic itself remains unread. This arrow identifies a contested intervention, not proof of its diagnosis or a general rejection of social history.
